content:
Have you ever turned on the radio and felt that every pop song sounds pretty much the same? Or watched a horror movie and figured out the ending after just 20 minutes?

Researchers from the Singapore Management University and James Cook University Singapore pointed out in a new paper published in the journal *Frontiers in Psychology* that "hyperselection" refers to the process in which, under intense competition, humans become increasingly adept at identifying and optimising what works, continuously selecting for the same traits and becoming reluctant to try other possibilities.

The result is impaired creativity. In a world that increasingly demands optimisation, "hyperselection" may make everything from music and urban planning to football matches more boring.

Research psychologist and lead author of the paper Jose C. Yong likened "hyperselection" to natural selection—the evolutionary process whereby individuals with advantageous traits or more effective strategies are more likely to survive and reproduce. Modern technology has made this selection process extremely rapid and intense.

Yong said: "We can now instantly identify what performs best, almost immediately copy it, and keep optimising. When there is strong selection pressure—for instance, intense competition or severe consequences for not optimising—this process gets accelerated."

Optimisation is generally useful because it helps us achieve our goals more efficiently. But when everyone optimises for the same thing, alternative traits, behaviours, products and strategies disappear. "Diversity and variability are traded away for efficiency, but that diversity and variability can actually be adaptive and useful."

When we fall into "hyperselection", we miss out on creative masterpieces like *Bohemian Rhapsody*.

When explaining the concept of "hyperselection" to people who have never heard of it, Yong likes to use Queen's *Bohemian Rhapsody* as an example. Although music critics in 1975 initially slammed the song as a "brazenly unoriginal pastiche" and a "stylistic collage that doesn't gel", the single is now considered one of the greatest rock songs of all time, largely because the band took creative risks.

"*Bohemian Rhapsody* is the opposite of 'hyperselection'."

Yong said: "The song is nearly six minutes long, spans wildly different musical sections, has no conventional chorus, and even features an operatic segment—these are all its hallmarks."

Another song that clearly does not fall under "hyperselection" is Stevie Nicks's *Edge of Seventeen*, which broke the typical song structure and has an extremely distinctive sound. Yong also mentioned System of a Down, noting that their songs sound "absolutely absurd" yet still managed to top the charts "because they are fresh and unique enough".

Compared with the past, today's radio pop hits could be described as derivative and dull—Yong could hardly even pick out a particular one as an example.

He said: "Honestly I'm not sure I can point to a contemporary pop song that exemplifies 'hyperselection', partly because so many pop songs nowadays sound alike and don't really leave a lasting impression."

But he said that certain music genres are textbook cases of "hyperselection", such as the low, mumbling, melancholic style of pop singers, or the mumble rap that was everywhere a few years ago.

Yong's co-author and fellow research psychologist Edison Tan has, because of "hyperselection", almost stopped listening to radio and instead seeks out lesser-known indie artists.

Tan told HuffPost: "It's not that my taste has changed—it's that the world has changed. What I crave is the richness and nuanced expression that pop music can no longer provide."

Yong said that, driven by streaming viewership data, commercial malleability, and the limited attention spans of social media, there is already a well-documented trend showing that music is becoming shorter and simpler.

Beyond music, where else can we see "hyperselection" at work?

Yong, Tan and their co-author Simon S. Groome believe that "hyperselection"—the pursuit of optimisation and efficiency—has made every aspect of life more predictable, more boring and more bland. They have also observed the phenomenon in the world of sport.

In professional football, teams are constantly looking for strategies to gain an edge. When a tactic proves successful, opponents quickly follow suit. Matches become more intense and tactics more sophisticated, but teams' playing styles are also increasingly similar, leaving less and less room for individual flair.

The same applies to working life. Tan uses the academic world, with which he is familiar, as an example.

He said: "As graduate students we were taught to break new ground, explore new ideas, and uncover how the world works."

In an ideal world, the best researchers should be the boldest, most creative problem-solvers—people willing to forge their own path. But reality is far from this ideal.

Tan said: "Scholars now have to prove their worth not by the quality of their ideas, but by metrics such as number of papers published, citation counts, and how much research funding they can raise."

He added: "The P in PhD no longer stands for Philosophy. When we see the same pattern emerging in every area of life, we have to ask: is there some fundamental force driving these trends?"

Artificial intelligence will accelerate the speed of "hyperselection"

It almost goes without saying that AI will accelerate "hyperselection". Yong said that AI is by design a process of recursive optimisation that requires almost no human intervention, and operates at a speed and scale far beyond what humans or any previous technology could achieve.

He said: "We're already starting to see this in online content—AI-generated articles, marketing copy, social media posts, images, videos, website designs, even music all feel eerily similar, because they are generated from the same underlying patterns and then continuously optimised for what works."

If people accept all of this content uncritically, there will be almost no check on AI-driven "hyperselection".

"Hyperselection" is not entirely bad, but creators need to be aware of its existence.

Yong stressed that optimisation itself is not a bad thing—it can help people achieve their goals and improve their lives. But because the pressure to optimise can be immense, creators may unwittingly sacrifice adaptive variation.

He said: "This is precisely where being aware of 'hyperselection' becomes crucial, and is part of the reason I want to spell out this concept. Only by recognising it can we think about what to do when it occurs."

Yong said the key is to be aware of how easily we fall into the trap of "hyperselection", and to find ways to nurture creativity and preserve diversity.

He said: "Creativity often comes from exposure to different things and recombining them in new ways. If everything looks, sounds and feels the same, we lose a treasure trove of alternative strategies and the raw material for new ideas."

We also need to be more thoughtful about the content we consume.

Yong said: "If audiences can recognise that music, films or other cultural products have become overly formulaic, and demand something more interesting, that in itself changes the selection pressures shaping production."
